gaps: Kpler and Vortexa publish different floating-storage scopes (Kpler ~29M bbl of floating crude Sep 8 vs Vortexa ~107M bbl of crude aboard tankers Aug 26); the two are not directly comparable, definitional difference, not a data conflict.
Iranian state media claimed August 2026 exports above $3B, a two-year high, while Vortexa/Kpler tracked only ~220-255 kb/d loaded that month, claimed vs tracked, unresolved.
The exact count of sanctioned vessels laden vs in ballast changes daily; no public source publishes it continuously.
Day-to-day vessel transit counts change constantly; Kpler/Vortexa snapshots cited are date-specific.
The Sep 21 struck tanker's name and flag were not released by UKMTO at time of reporting.
Whether the Sep 22 LNG tanker strike is independently confirmed beyond UKMTO/DPA reporting.
EIA's next scheduled World Oil Transit Chokepoints update date was not found.
Exact current daily barrel flow (vs vessel counts), trackers report vessels; EIA's quarterly volume series lags by months.
Two outlets report EIA's Q1 2026 Hormuz figure as 14.9 million b/d rather than 14.6; the decomposed breakdown (10.7 crude plus 3.9 products) sums to 14.6, which is used here.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Fox News that Hormuz flows were averaging almost 13 million b/d with a single day above 20 million; single-outlet report, not corroborated against tracker data, so it is not used in the table.
No single verified series for daily Bab el-Mandeb oil volume in September 2026, trackers report vessel counts, EIA reports quarterly volumes with a lag.
Houthi merchant-ship count claims (408 ships Sep 11–21) are self-reported and not independently verified.
Exact per-route freight surcharge pass-through to delivered crude prices is estimated, not measured.
No verified current count of how many Houthi attacks on vessels have occurred in 2026 specifically targeting tankers vs other shipping.
No independent confirmation of Houthi tanker-hit claims (Wafa, Amzan) or the claimed tally of eight Saudi tankers struck and 29 turned back.
Repair timeline for the East-West Pipeline pumping stations is unverified; estimates range from weeks to six-plus weeks and the effective restart rate is unknown.
No public breakdown of where Saudi Gulf-terminal loadings went during the Petroline outage, limiting the Europe-vs-Asia crude split read.

watches.title: Russian Refining Watch
watches.dek: Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian refining: strikes, offline capacity, and the diesel crisis.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the diesel side of the crude market: Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries remove products, not crude, so the read is crack spreads and export curbs rather than wellhead output. Ukrainian claims are carried as claims. Strike dates are approximate and every bullet carries its vintage.
watches.wcs_stakes: Russian refinery outages tighten global diesel, and record diesel cracks keep US and Asian refiners running at maximum to capture them, which is the demand-side bid under heavy sour barrels including Western Canadian Select (WCS). At the same time, crude displaced from downed Russian refineries has pushed seaborne Russian exports to 16-month highs, capping how much support the tight product market can pass back to sour crude prices. The net effect for WCS is constructive while diesel cracks stay extreme: refineries run hard and bid for every discounted heavy barrel they can crack.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, watch the diesel crack, not the strike count: it is the margin that decides how hard refiners run and how much they pay for heavy barrels. If an energy ceasefire returns Russian refineries and the diesel crack compresses, runs fall and discounted heavies strand first. Until then, the tight product market is the best demand cover WCS has.

bullets.text: Russia's Transport Ministry said naval drones struck the Liberian-flagged crude tanker Aframax Rio off the resort city of Sochi on Oct 6, with crude burning openly on the Black Sea; all 23 crew, all Indian nationals, were rescued with no reported injuries. Kyiv had listed the vessel as part of Russia's shadow fleet used to move Russian oil under Western sanctions.

Overnight strikes on Oct 3-4 hit the Lazarevo pumping station on the Surgut-Gorky-Polotsk crude pipeline in the Kirov region, sparked a large fire at the Saratov refinery on the Volga, and set a fuel depot ablaze in Matveyev Kurgan; Moscow-appointed authorities in Crimea restricted gasoline sales without stating a reason.

The Black Sea export port of Novorossiysk suspended oil exports for several days after a major Ukrainian attack on the port early on Oct 2, the same Reuters-sourced reporting said, as Ukraine's campaign widened from refineries to export terminals.

Two merchant vessels were hit by air and sea drones around 3 a.m. on Oct 6 inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, about 112 km off Byala; the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sank with its crew missing and the Palau-flagged Able caught fire, with 18 crew rescued and two injured. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev confirmed the attack, the first on shipping in Bulgarian waters, and called it a gross violation of international law; no party has claimed responsibility.

Bloomberg tanker-tracking data cited by OilPrice.com show Russia's seaborne crude exports averaged 3.62 million barrels per day in the four weeks to September 28, the highest since May 2024, a sign that neither India nor other major buyers have reduced purchases despite US pressure. Russia's oil and gas revenues were nevertheless expected to plunge 23 percent year on year in September on lower crude prices and a stronger ruble, per Reuters calculations cited in the piece.
bullets.vintage: Data: four weeks ending Sep 28, 2026; accessed 2026-09-24

bullets.text: The Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, the main western outlet for displaced crude, is itself constrained: trader data show exports and transit volumes more than halved from July to August, from 800,000 barrels per day to less than 355,000, after repeated drone strikes collapsed loadings and thinned tanker availability. Chartering a Suezmax tanker to India from Novorossiysk cost about $20 million by the end of August, versus about $13 million a month earlier.

Russian diesel cargoes are returning to their main previous customers following the US-brokered lifting of Moscow's export ban, with at least two tankers signalling voyages to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, Reuters reported on Oct 20, citing shipping data from Kpler and LSEG. The tanker Leruo is signalling Manaus, Brazil, after departing the Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct 16, following the tanker Dolunay, which left Primorsk with a diesel cargo on Oct 14 bound for Alanya, Turkey. Turkey has received about 34 percent of Russian diesel loadings so far this year at 95,000 b/d and Brazil about 24 percent at 66,000 b/d, Kpler data show. Russia partially lifted the diesel export ban starting Oct 10; it had reduced exports over the summer before imposing the ban as it grappled with widespread Ukrainian attacks on its oil refineries.

Russia's crude oil production increased by 65,000 b/d in September to 8.43 million b/d, but remained about 870,000 b/d below a year ago, Reuters reported on Oct 20, citing the International Energy Agency's assessment published last week. The year-on-year shortfall sits alongside the refinery outage campaign and the diesel export disruption tracked on this page.

Oil prices fell on Oct 19 as traders weighed possibly higher Russian supplies after US sanctions relief on Friday, Reuters reported, with Brent crude futures down $2.29, or 2.08 percent, to $107.57 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate down $1.95, or 1.92 percent, to $99.46, both pulling back from five-month highs settled on Friday. The waiver follows the deal Trump struck with President Putin for Russia to export diesel to the United States and other countries, starting at about 2.3 million barrels this month before rising to about 7.6 million barrels monthly, Reuters said, adding that Zelenskiy said the US actions will hurt Ukraine and that analysts said mixed messaging on the waiver's details and duration has created uncertainty, so the market is unlikely to fully price in a sustained increase in supply.

President Trump's waiver of Russian sanctions eases energy concerns for India, one of the top importers of Russian oil, and may improve the chances of New Delhi and Washington agreeing on a trade deal, Reuters reported on Oct 19. The Graham Act legislation would have exposed Indian goods to tariffs of up to 100 percent, as India is one of the five largest importers of Russian oil. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who arrives in India on Tuesday, said trade talks with New Delhi were a consideration for Trump's waiver decision and that the two sides are very close to finalising a trade deal. Earlier this year Russia accounted for nearly half of India's oil imports, but purchases fell in August and continue to decline, Reuters said.

President Zelenskiy said on Oct 18 that Russia had deliberately launched at least 76 attacks on energy or oil and gas targets over the past week, including overnight strikes on substations in four regions, and that tens of thousands of families remained without power. Over the week Russia attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, Zelenskiy said.

President Trump said on Oct 17 that he had not announced a final decision on the Russia sanctions he waived a day earlier, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president will take up to 60 days to weigh the economic impact before deciding what comes next, Reuters reported. The Oct 16 executive order used the Graham Act's waiver power to set aside most of the law's new sanctions and its duties, a 500 percent duty on Russian goods and 100 percent duties on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, which were due to take effect Oct 18; sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders remain in place, and Zelenskyy condemned the waiver.

Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said on Oct 16 that the US Treasury has asked Russia's sovereign wealth fund, the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), which he heads, to facilitate payments relating to the Trump-Putin deal on the sale of Russian diesel. Dmitriev told an energy conference the Treasury had requested RDIF to facilitate payments and solve tactical issues, and said RDIF will work to ensure that all payments are efficient and reach their intended recipients.

Russia publicly acknowledged the Oct 15 Ukrainian drone strike on the Ryazan refinery on Oct 16 and state TV channel Rossiya-24 broadcast images of the aftermath, the first time state television has shown a refinery attack since the war began, Reuters reported. Moscow is highlighting an attack President Trump has called a disgrace, four days after he announced an energy ceasefire that neither side confirmed; Ukraine said it paused strikes for three days and resumed because Russia kept hitting Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leaving 600,000 people without power on Oct 14.

Attacks on Russian refineries have cut an estimated one million tonnes a month of fuel oil supply, Vitol's Asia head Kieran Gallagher said at the SIBCON conference this week, while high-sulphur fuel oil flows through Hormuz, including Iranian supplies, remain down by at least 800,000 tonnes a month from February. Spot premiums for 380-cst high-sulphur fuel oil held near $50 a tonne this week, versus a $5.10 premium on Feb 27, on LSEG data.

Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian refineries on Oct 15 after a three-day pause, President Zelenskiy told the Financial Times, saying the block on energy strikes was over because Russia kept hitting Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leaving 600,000 people without power on Oct 14. The Ryazan hit was the first Ukrainian attack on a Russian energy facility since President Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Oct 11, a truce neither side confirmed; Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no specific agreements had been established.

The IEA said on Oct 14 that a lack of operational Russian refinery capacity meant the recently announced easing of Russian diesel export restrictions was unlikely to bring any material change to the global gasoil balance, and that constrained diesel supplies could persist well into next year. The agency put Russian crude production in September at 8.43 million b/d, up 65,000 b/d on the month but 870,000 b/d below a year earlier.

President Zelenskiy said on Oct 13 that Ukraine had carried out no strikes on Russian oil refineries or other energy sites in the two days since the Oct 11 US announcement of an energy ceasefire, while accusing Russia of continuing to hit Ukrainian energy facilities over the same period.

President Zelenskiy said on Oct 12 that Russia had hit at least six Ukrainian energy targets in overnight strikes despite the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump, and that Moscow had shown no interest in accepting it. The Kremlin was reported as saying it does not want a ceasefire. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, Moscow's point man for oil, said Russia would be able to return diesel exports to levels above those outlined in the Trump diesel deal.

On Oct 11 Trump posted that an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine was effective immediately, with neither government confirming any deal. Zelensky said Ukraine would honor it if Russia reciprocated, but Russian strikes on Ukrainian power facilities continued afterward and the Kremlin made no public commitment.

Axios, citing a US official, reported Trump moved ahead with the Russian diesel waiver after Zelensky ignored about six US requests to stop hitting Russian refineries; during Oct 9 talks in Miami, envoys Witkoff and Kushner told Ukraine's delegation the waiver was coming because the strikes were 'directly affecting U.S. consumers'.

President Trump said after a phone call with Vladimir Putin that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons 'immediately thereafter,' and 3 million more 'within a short period.' Treasury immediately issued a general license sparing Russian diesel loaded as of Oct 9 from sanctions until April 2027, the first diesel easing longer than the standard 30-day window; Deputy PM Novak told Tass Russia is lifting diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule, with US-bound supplies possible in October. The IEA says Russian diesel output has fallen about 30% amid the strikes.

Russia's State Duma budget and tax committee backed draft Tax Code amendments extending an existing fuel-import subsidy to large-scale seaborne gasoline imports from India, with the subsidy calculated off an indicative Indian gasoline price plus shipping costs. Operating refineries are producing about 85,000 tonnes of gasoline per day against demand of around 111,000 tonnes, leaving a structural shortfall near 25,000 tonnes a day, roughly 20% of consumption.
bullets.source: Investment Guru India (via Kyiv Post, citing RBC)

bullets.text: In a rare acknowledgment at the Oct 1 Valdai Club session, Putin said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries had cost Russia roughly 1% of GDP and conceded Kyiv had partially achieved its goal of damaging the economy, while offering no ceasefire and saying Russia would prefer talks.

A fire broke out at an oil pumping station near Michurinsk in Russia's Tambov Oblast after an overnight drone attack on Oct 20, according to Telegram monitoring channels reported by the Kyiv Independent via EuropeSays. Tambov Oblast Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov said a Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire on the territory of one of the enterprises in Michurinsky District without naming the facility, claimed four drones were shot down, and reported no casualties. Independent Russian outlet ASTRA said the fire likely started at the Nikolskoye-1 linear production and dispatch station near Novonikolskoye, a Transneft facility on the Druzhba pipeline network about 350 to 400 kilometres from the front line, which Ukraine previously attacked on Aug 18, 2025, when the strike halted Druzhba operation. Ukrainian authorities did not confirm the attack and the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify a fire at the station.

Reports on Oct 20 confirmed the damage from the Oct 17-18 Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg, Tank Storage Magazine reported: at the St. Petersburg oil terminal, three storage tanks caught fire, with two damaged and one completely destroyed; at the Ruchyi oil depot, one vertical steel tank was destroyed and another damaged. A large scale fire at the Ozon logistics hub affected more than 10,000 square metres, and the Southern Fairway Bridge and the Finland Railway Bridge were both damaged. One person was confirmed killed and 15 others injured in the overall attack, which involved over 1,000 drones launched at the terminal, the depot, the logistics hub and the bridges.

The St. Petersburg oil terminal struck on Oct 18 exports about 120,000 b/d of refined products, mostly fuel oil, according to data from Kpler cited by CNBC on Oct 19, and it is unclear how bad the damage at the facility is. Ukraine briefly paused strikes on Russian energy facilities after President Trump declared on Oct 11 that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to a truce, but Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure after that announcement and President Zelenskiy said last week Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian facilities in retaliation.

Ukraine launched one of the largest drone attacks of the war overnight Oct 17-18, striking the St. Petersburg oil terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot, with fires also reported at industrial warehouses in the city's Kolpinsky District, St. Petersburg governor Alexander Beglov said. One person was killed and five injured in St. Petersburg, and two transformer substations struck at Yanino in the Leningrad region left about 20,000 people without electricity on Sunday morning. Russia's Defence Ministry said air defences shot down some 1,015 drones near Moscow and several other western regions.

Reuters reported on Oct 16, citing unnamed industry sources, that Rosneft's Ryazan refinery suspended operations at one of its main crude distillation units, CDU-6, following the drone attack on Oct 15. The same unit had already been shut after a drone strike in September. The refinery's three other primary crude distillation units, CDU-1, CDU-3 and CDU-4, reportedly continue to operate.

A large Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire at Rosneft's Ryazan refinery early on Oct 15, regional governor Pavel Malkov said, with damage still being assessed and emergency services at the scene. The plant, about 300 km southeast of Moscow, supplies fuel to the capital and accounts for almost 5 percent of Russian refining throughput; it has been hit several times in recent months.

Ukraine's Ministry of Defence said its forces hit 12 large Russian refineries in September, per ArmyInform reporting on Oct 12, with Lukoil's Perm refinery, about 1,500 km from the border, the farthest on the list. Monitoring by Euromaidan Press found no reports of new Ukrainian refinery strikes in the sources it tracks since the Oct 11 ceasefire announcement.

Ukraine's military confirmed long-range drones struck Tatneft's TANECO refinery at Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan on Oct 12, about 750 miles from the Ukrainian border, as part of a wider attack on industrial targets in the region. Tatarstan's leader said the attack killed at least 13 people, including a child, and wounded 39. TANECO processed 17 million tons of crude in 2024, producing 2.7 million tons of gasoline and 8.5 million tons of diesel, and had been hit before in early June.

Three of Russia's six largest diesel-producing refineries are now shut or running at roughly one-quarter capacity, according to Reuters calculations cited Oct 12: Kirishi is completely offline, Volgograd and NORSI are at about 25 percent of nameplate, and TANECO was struck on Sunday Oct 11. The six plants, Omsk, Kirishi, TANECO, Volgograd, NORSI and Perm, together account for roughly half of Russian diesel production.

Ukraine struck the Samara linear production and dispatch station, a Transneft Urals-blend hub, for the third time this month overnight Oct 9-10; the Ukrainian General Staff said the earlier Oct 2 and Oct 7 hits caused extensive damage to storage tanks and associated infrastructure at the junction.

Ukrainian drones struck the Novoshakhtinsk/Yug Rusi oil-loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don overnight Oct 9-10, starting a major fire at the export-loading facility; the regional governor confirmed two ships damaged at the Port of Azov and a rail bridge strike in the same wave.

Ukraine attacked Lukoil's Ukhta oil-processing plant in the Komi Republic, the fourth Russian refinery hit this week after Omsk, Salavat and the Astrakhan gas plant, President Zelenskyy confirmed Friday; the plant's design capacity is about 80,000 b/d, and Bloomberg calculates the four facilities hit this week total about 720,000 b/d of crude capacity plus up to 12 Bcm per year of gas.

Ukraine's General Staff said it struck Russia's largest refinery, the Gazprom Neft Omsk plant (about 440,000 b/d, roughly one-fifteenth of national capacity), overnight Oct 8, some 2,500-2,700 km from Ukraine; regional governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed a drone hit an industrial zone. It is the second strike on Omsk since July 6, and Zelenskyy called it an 'important achievement,' saying 'Siberia, too, is now within reach.'

In the same overnight wave, Ukraine's military said it struck the Ust-Luga and Vysotsk ports, which handle Baltic Sea oil exports, plus targets in the Kaluga and Yaroslavl regions, with local governors confirming the attacks; the strikes widen the campaign from refineries to export infrastructure.

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Oct 8 that the Oct 2 strike on the Samara linear production and dispatch station at Prosvet damaged 11 RVS-20000 tanks, 3 RVS-50000 tanks, pipeline sections and an automated oil loading station; the hub blends Urals export crude and, per the General Staff, handles up to half of Russia's oil exports.

Ukraine's General Staff claimed an overnight strike on the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat refinery complex in Bashkortostan, described as one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities, about 750 miles east of Moscow; local authorities had not confirmed the claim. The 200 kb/d plant was previously hit on July 14 and September 24, when its AVT-6 primary unit caught fire.

President Zelenskyy said on Oct 7 that Ukrainian forces struck two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions over the past day, calling them 'justified responses' to Russian strikes on Ukraine.

Rosneft's Ryazan refinery, Russia's fourth-largest at more than 260,000 b/d, suspended crude processing after a weekend drone attack; Reuters industry sources said the plant is expected to stay idle until the end of the month with no product loadings planned before Dec 1, and a second crude unit is under repair after an earlier strike that took about 80,000 b/d offline.

Overnight on Oct 5-6, Ukraine launched what Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin called one of the largest drone attacks on the capital region in two years, with about 650 drones approaching and 105 downed near the city; the regional governor reported one fatality and six injured. Monitoring channels and eyewitness footage showed flames and heavy smoke at the Volodarskaya linear production and dispatch station near Konstantinovo, Transneft's largest Moscow-region oil depot at about 3 million tons a year, which supplies fuel to the capital's three main airports; Russian authorities have not confirmed damage at the depot itself.
bullets.source: The Gaze (citing Astra and eyewitness footage)

bullets.text: Ukraine's General Staff said a drone strike ignited fires at the port of Taman in the Krasnodar region, damaging an oil storage tank, a warehouse and terminals, with regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev reporting two people wounded. The same statement said a Pantsir-S1 air defense system in occupied Crimea was also hit.

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed the October 1-2 strikes on the Lukoil-Volgogradneftepererabotka refinery, one of Russia's largest at about 15 million tons per year, and on Transneft's Samara tank farm plus the Samara-1 and Samara-2 pumping stations; analysts described the Samara facility as Europe's largest tank farm. Russia's defense ministry claimed to have intercepted 646 drones in the same overnight wave.

Coordinated Ukrainian strikes overnight hit the LUKOIL-Volgograd refinery and the Samara oil dispatch station near Prosvet, Ukrainian authorities said. Explosions and fires were recorded at both sites; NASA's FIRMS satellite service registered fire hotspots at key processing units of the Volgograd refinery, which handles about 15 million tons of crude a year and has been repeatedly targeted. The Samara station blends different crude grades into Russia's main Urals export stream and was previously struck in April, when five crude tanks were damaged.
Russia's second-largest refinery, Kirishi, halted processing on September 29 after Ukrainian drone attacks damaged three of its four crude distillation units, two industry sources told Reuters.

Russia raised its expected idle primary refining capacity for October by 67% versus the earlier plan to 4.0 million tons, per Reuters industry-source estimates, after postponed maintenance at Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk refinery and a unit of Lukoil's NORSI; Rosneft's Tuapse refinery also reportedly halted crude processing on Oct 1 on low margins. More than half of October's idle capacity is expected to return in November, with November idle at 1.2 to 1.8 million tons.

The Associated Press reported on Oct 4 that the International Energy Agency estimates a Russian refinery has been successfully struck by a drone roughly once every three days in recent months. The cadence is consistent with a sustained attrition campaign but is not an independent confirmation of Ukraine's claim, which AP noted it could not verify, that 51% of Russian refining capacity is out of action.

Ukraine's Defence Ministry said on October 4 that long-range strikes have put 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity out of action, citing strikes on refineries in Moscow, Yaroslavl, Perm, Saratov and Syzran plus the Kirishi (Kinef) and Ust-Luga plants. The claim could not be independently verified. President Vladimir Putin told the Valdai forum on October 1 that the strikes had cost Russia about 1% of gross domestic product (GDP), while International Energy Agency (IEA) data cited in the report says Russian diesel output has fallen about 30%, with drivers queuing up to 40 hours at filling stations and Moscow banning diesel exports.

Ukraine's Defense Intelligence representative Andrii Yusov said Ukrainian forces have conducted 64 targeted strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure facilities this year, destroying or damaging about one-third of the targeted refineries and storage facilities, and said the strikes compound Western sanctions that restrict imports of repair equipment. The agency framed the disruption as long-term pressure on Russian military logistics. This is a Ukrainian claim, not independently verified.

gaps: Russian government has not published confirmed damage figures; offline estimates are Western/industry estimates or Ukrainian claims.
Repair timelines reported by sources (weeks to months) are not independently verifiable.
Whether repair times are lengthening due to sanctions on replacement equipment could not be verified from a primary source.
No confirmed independent series for Russia's actual monthly refinery throughput in 2026 beyond IEA estimates.

No public reconciliation between the International Energy Agency's June throughput estimate (3.8 million barrels per day) and JPMorgan's current sub-5-million estimate; the two may use different definitions, and the gap matters for judging how fast capacity is being lost.

No public data on how much crude displaced from downed refineries is being rerouted to export terminals versus going into storage, or whether port and shadow-fleet tanker capacity cap the redirection.
Whether market talk of possible U.S. diesel export restrictions (flagged in commentary around September 23) reflects real policy discussion could not be verified from an official source.

watches.title: China Import Watch
watches.dek: China's crude buying: import volumes, sourcing shifts, teapot run rates, and what it means for sour barrel demand.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the buy side of the sour barrel: China's import volumes and refinery runs decide how much sour crude Asia pulls, and the stock math (imports plus domestic production minus throughput) shows whether Beijing is building inventories or drawing them. Every bullet carries its vintage, so read 2026 wartime figures against pre-war baselines rather than against last week alone.
watches.wcs_stakes: China's buying is rotating, not growing: Russian and Iranian crude fell below one-third of September imports from about half in August (Goldman Sachs), and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says only about 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remain on the water under the US blockade -- a forced shift toward non-sanctioned sour that bids up the grades Western Canadian Select (WCS) competes with. But the bid is selective: seaborne imports sit almost 3 million b/d below normal seasonal levels even as refineries processed 13.91 million b/d in August, the most since March. Watch the Kayrros satellite inventory reads and the monthly throughput numbers: restocking bids up sour, stock draws soften the WCS basis.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, China matters through the sour barrel, not through direct Canadian sales. Strong Chinese runs and restocking bid up the grades Mars and Urals price against, which keeps the Canadian differential tight; a stock draw and a buying pause do the opposite. The teapot substitution story, Urals and fuel oil standing in for blocked Iranian barrels, is the near-term variable to watch.

bullets.text: China's crude oil imports fell 21.5 percent from a year earlier in September to 37.1 million tonnes, or 9.03 million barrels per day, customs data showed, though the daily rate edged up 1.1 percent from August, Reuters reported on Oct 14. Imports for the first nine months of 2026 totalled 357.97 million tonnes, or 9.57 million barrels per day, down 15.3 percent from the same period last year. September seaborne imports stood at 7.6 million barrels per day, down from 9.9 million a year earlier, according to Vortexa, with Iranian oil arrivals down to 0.5 million barrels per day.
bullets.vintage: Data: Sep 2026 customs; published Oct 14, 2026; accessed 2026-10-19

bullets.text: FGE NexantECA and Energy Aspects cut their fourth-quarter China crude import forecasts by about 400,000 b/d, now expecting 9.2 to 9.3 million b/d versus last year's average of 11.6 million b/d, OilPrice.com reported on Sep 30. September imports were expected near August levels, with the arriving cargoes bought when prices were in the $80s before Brent held above $100; August imports were still 23.4% below a year earlier, improved from June's decade low of 7.1 million b/d. OilPrice quoted FGE NexantECA's Samuel Kong saying no significant upside is expected as hefty premiums and record-high freight erode margins, and reported the teapots could start reducing runs as Iranian and Venezuelan supply dries up under US sanctions.

Goldman Sachs estimated China's seaborne crude net imports rose about 6 percent in September from August but stayed almost 3 million barrels per day below normal seasonal levels, and its models point to only about 600,000 barrels per day more total crude imports in the fourth quarter versus the third. The bank estimates a sustained 1 million barrel per day change in China's net crude imports over six months would shift Brent's fair value by about 4 dollars a barrel.

Reuters columnist Clyde Russell's analysis of official data (published Sep 15, 2026) showed China processed 13.91 million b/d in August, the most since March, against 8.93 million b/d of imports plus 4.34 million b/d of domestic production, implying a 640,000 b/d inventory draw. It was the third draw in four months (draws of 500,000 b/d in May and 940,000 b/d in June, a 210,000 b/d surplus in July); stocks are estimated at at least 1.2 billion barrels, and January to August still showed a net surplus of 330,000 b/d.

Kpler data cited by Maritime Professional (Sep 23, 2026) put Asia on course to import 23.96 million b/d of crude in September, up from 23.38 million in August and the highest since February, extending the recovery from April's decade-plus low. Even so, September remained 13% below the 27.55 million b/d three-month pre-conflict average through February.
bullets.vintage: Prelim data: Sep 2026; published Sep 23, 2026; accessed 2026-09-24

bullets.text: Kpler data showed India remained the largest buyer of Russian crude in September at about 1.82 million barrels per day, but its intake fell roughly 29 percent from July as Chinese refiners stepped up purchases and tightened availability, HDFC Sky reported on Oct 14. China took about 1.49 million barrels per day of Russian crude in September, and Kpler's Sumit Ritolia said Chinese refiners have drawn more Russian barrels in recent months partly because of reduced access to Iranian crude, adding to competition for the available supply.

Kpler data cited by Reuters on Oct 6 showed China's imports of Iranian oil nearly halved in September from a year earlier to 590,000 barrels per day, the lowest since January 2023, and Iran exported no crude at all in September for the first time since Kpler began tracking flows in 2013. The volume of Iranian crude stored on vessels outside the blockade zone has more than halved to 45 million barrels from 100 million barrels in late July, Kpler said. Reuters also reported that Bloomberg found at least 50 tankers, mostly carrying Iranian crude, bottled up off China's coast, and that Russian ESPO was commanding a premium of almost $30 a barrel above Brent, pricing most independent refiners out of Russian barrels while state-owned refiners took most of the available Russian crude.

Reuters reported on Oct 6 that Chinese independent refiners stepped up purchases of crude from Iraq and Qatar for October and November delivery to replace dwindling Iranian supplies, as exports from other Gulf producers through the Strait of Hormuz recover. Three traders told Reuters the refiners bought at least 12 million barrels of Iraqi and Qatari crude from trading houses Mercuria, Totsa and Trafigura, with one estimating total purchases of 15 to 20 million barrels. The cargoes sold at premiums of $12 to about $20 a barrel to the ICE Brent benchmark on a delivered basis; most were Iraqi Basra Medium and Heavy, among the cheapest Middle East grades available. Buyers included Hongrun Petrochemical, Qicheng Petrochemical, Qirun Petrochemical, Hualong and Chambroad Petrochemical, and Hongrun and Shenchi Petrochemical also bought 3 million barrels of Qatar's al-Shaheen crude for early-November arrival. One trader told Reuters that Iraqi oil has become the new benchmark for China's independent refiners because supplies are ample and can be obtained quickly. The deals followed purchases of more than 20 million barrels of crude from West Africa, Canada and Colombia between late August and early September as Iranian supply dwindled after the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian vessels in July.

Saudi Arabia unexpectedly cut its November crude prices for Asia to six-year lows while raising them for northwest Europe, Reuters reported, closing a question the watch had carried into October. Aramco set November Arab Light to Asia at $5 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average, down $3 from October, the widest discount since June 2020; Arab Medium and Arab Heavy to Asia were cut $5 a barrel. The cuts defied a Reuters survey expecting up to a $5 a barrel hike, and refining sources told Reuters they were aimed at compensating Asian buyers for record freight costs (VLCC Gulf to China at $1.2 million a day, per LSEG data) and protecting Aramco's market share after the war disrupted exports.

Russian and Iranian crude accounted for less than one-third of China's September imports, down from about half in August, as China shifted toward non-sanctioned supply, per Goldman Sachs analysis. The bank said the shift toward openly traded crude could make changes in Chinese purchasing more visible in benchmark pricing.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Fox News interview on Sep 27 that only about 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remain on the water under the US blockade, with final deliveries to China expected within about two weeks, after which he claimed Iran would have nothing left to trade. That is an unverified prediction from the official directing the sanctions effort, not independent evidence that Iranian exports have stopped.

TankerTrackers reported Sep 24 that almost 6 million barrels of confiscated Iranian crude, including the 1.88-million-barrel tanker Majestic X seized in the Indian Ocean in April while headed for China, were crossing the Atlantic toward the United States. The report relies on a single tracking source and should be treated as a lead until corroborated.
bullets.vintage: TankerTrackers report Sep 24, 2026; published Sep 26, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: Saudi Aramco cut its September official selling price (OSP) for Arab Light to Asia by 50 cents a barrel to a $2/bbl discount against the regional benchmark, the fifth-lowest differential since 2000, per Energies Media (Aug 19, 2026). The cut reflected war-driven costs (freight, rerouting) plus formal discount requests from Asian refiners for longer voyages; Aramco held exports near 5 million b/d, about 70% of normal, leaning on Red Sea port Yanbu and potentially Sidi Kerir loadings.

Saudi Arabia left its October-loading Arab Light official selling price (OSP) to Asia unchanged, according to Reuters reporting via TradingView on Sep 3, 2026, pausing the easing that had taken the September price to a $2/bbl discount against the regional benchmark.

Reuters columnist Gavin Maguire wrote on Oct 5 that China's suspension of fuel exports for October left India best placed to fill the resulting hole in Asian fuel supply. Citing Kpler data, he reported India has 23 refineries able to process about 5.6 million b/d and was the larger fuel exporter in 2025 (about 47 million tonnes of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel versus China's 25.4 million), though India's fuel exports in the first nine months of 2026 were down roughly 23%, or about 8 million tonnes, year on year. He noted two recent cuts to India's fuel-export taxes and a rebound in Middle East crude deliveries to India, which hit 11.3 million tonnes in September, the highest since February, as signs India can step back into the export market.
bullets.source: Reuters (Gavin Maguire commentary; reprinted by The Hindu Business Line)

bullets.text: Crux Investor reported on Oct 1 that Chinese refiners had suspended refined-product exports beyond Hong Kong and Macau with no stated end date, sending December Brent futures up 2.4% to $100.36 a barrel while the expiring November contract settled at $103.50. The report noted Middle East crude exports had recovered to 17.5 million b/d, 98% of prewar levels, even as US distillate inventories fell 2.3 million barrels to 105.2 million, 14% below the five-year average. The export suspension was corroborated by a Reuters columnist on Oct 5.

Gasoline inventories at state-owned majors fell 2.9 percent in a week to their lowest since 2022 and diesel stocks hit a 15-month low after a 2.4 percent drop, per commodity research firm JLC International cited by Bloomberg. Energy Aspects analyst Jiana Sun told Bloomberg there is a growing risk Beijing caps monthly clean product exports at about 1.2 million tons in the fourth quarter.

Energy News Beat (Sep 13, 2026) reported the second batch of 2026 clean-product export quotas brought China's total 2026 allocation to about 32 million tonnes. August product exports hit 6.01 million tonnes, up 12.7% year on year, but January to August exports were still down 9.6% year on year, with gasoline down 57% year to date, consistent with a policy-managed surplus rather than an unconstrained export boom.

General Administration of Customs (GAC) data reported by IDNFinancials (Sep 18, 2026) gave August per-fuel detail: gasoline exports 700,000 tonnes, down 17.5% year on year but the highest since October 2025; diesel 1.33 million tonnes, up 42.1% year on year and the highest since March 2024; jet fuel a record 2.55 million tonnes, up 41.4% year on year. Liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports fell 17.8% year on year to 5.16 million tonnes.

Baird Maritime (Sep 21, 2026, citing GAC customs data) reported China's August fuel oil exports fell to 1.21 million tonnes (about 247,000 b/d), down 35% month on month and 27% year on year, the lowest since October 2024, partly on weather disruption at the Zhoushan bunkering hub. Fuel oil imports were 1.3 million tonnes, up 15% month on month and down 11% year on year; crude throughput climbed for a second month, supported by stronger fuel exports after Beijing eased export restrictions in mid-July.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 9 that record-high freight costs have effectively shut the US Gulf to Asia crude arbitrage, with Asian refiners turning to more barrels from the Middle East and South America, shipbrokers and traders told Reuters. Trafigura chartered a supertanker to ship crude from the US Gulf Coast to China at a lump-sum fee of $76 million, a source told CNBC, about ten times the $7 to $10 million before the war, implying freight costs of about $38 per barrel. Rates on the US Gulf to Japan route are also surging, with one supertanker offered at $82 million, up 50% from three weeks earlier, Bloomberg reported. With the US-Asia arbitrage closed, Asian refiners are considering more of the UAE's Murban grade, pushing its premium over Dubai quotes above $11 per barrel on Thursday.

Baltic Exchange data put the time charter equivalent for a 270,000-ton very large crude carrier (VLCC) on the TD3C Middle East Gulf to China route at about 1.212 million dollars per day on Sep 17, up from about 1.034 million the day before and roughly 700,000 at the start of September. The Baltic's Sep 18 weekly report put TD3C at Worldscale 1,140, the Gulf of Oman to China TD34 route at 870,947 dollars per day, and West Africa to China TD15 at 524,575 dollars per day.

The 2016-built VLCC Kuwait Prosperity, operated by Sinokor, was fixed at Worldscale 1,350 for a Persian Gulf to east voyage loading by Total Singapore on Sep 22, with a daily equivalent estimated above 1 million dollars. Analysts attribute the spike to reduced Hormuz transits, longer voyages via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, and diversions around the Cape of Good Hope adding an estimated 11 to 14 million dollars per voyage in charter costs alone.
bullets.vintage: Fixture for Sep 22 loading; reported Sep 21, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

bullets.text: Tide Signal News (Sep 23, 2026, citing Reuters/Baltic Exchange data) reported very large crude carrier (VLCC) freight from the Gulf of Oman to China hit Worldscale 450, about $11.50 per barrel, a record for the route and up roughly 65% from the Sep 4 TD34 assessment, as conflict risk shrank the pool of tankers willing to trade around the Gulf.

Vessel Hunter News (Sep 22, 2026, citing Baltic Exchange data) reported the TD3C Middle East Gulf to China very large crude carrier (VLCC) time-charter equivalent reached $1.2125 million a day on Sep 17, up 40.6% on the week and roughly ten times the $117,400 a day before the February conflict. TD15 West Africa to Far East hit $524,500 a day and TD22 US Gulf to Far East $388,400 a day; the China Crude Oil Tanker Freight Index stood at 14,575 points on Sep 16, about 83% above its early-September level.
bullets.source: Vessel Hunter News (citing Baltic Exchange data)

bullets.text: Reuters reported on Oct 6 that Shandong refinery utilization fell to about 55% by late September from nearly 60% at the start of the month, per consultancy Horizon Insights, as margins deteriorated after China capped fuel price increases while crude feedstock costs surged. Refiners were losing 250 to 500 yuan per metric ton by late September, compared with profits of about 500 yuan per ton in early September. One trader said buyers were unwilling to pay spot premiums above $20 a barrel. Kpler senior analyst Muyu Xu said inventories at some Shandong teapots could run out as early as the end of October and that refiners need to secure alternative supplies to avoid shutting down or cutting run rates significantly.

The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air's August 2026 snapshot (published Sep 17, 2026) found refinery throughput down 6.9% year on year in August, though recovered from July's slump. New energy vehicle (NEV) output rose 21.9% year on year to 61% of all vehicles produced, and battery production surged 70% year on year, consistent with continued structural gasoline displacement.
bullets.source: Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air

bullets.text: The weak September arrivals forced the largest draw on China's onshore crude inventories in the trackers' records: Vortexa counted a 57 million barrel draw in September and Kpler a 47.5 million barrel draw, the biggest monthly declines since their series began in 2019 and 2017 respectively, Reuters reported on Oct 14. Vortexa's Emma Li attributed the draw to Middle East shipping disruptions, mainly ship-to-ship transfer bottlenecks around Hormuz, delaying cargoes due in late August and September. Kpler pegged China's fourth-quarter seaborne crude imports at 8.0 to 8.5 million barrels per day.

The US Energy Information Administration (EIA), in analysis published April 2026, classifies China's strategic oil inventories at an estimated 1.397 billion barrels, comprising about 360 million barrels government-held and 1 billion barrels commercial. The EIA treats both as strategic because China's national oil companies have reportedly been instructed since 2024 to hold emergency oil in commercial tanks.

Geospatial firm Kayrros, via MEXC reporting from the Asia Pacific Petroleum Conference (APPEC) in Singapore, estimated China's strategic petroleum reserve (SPR) at about 415 million barrels and commercial stocks at about 780 million barrels in early September 2026, up close to 130 million barrels combined since late March, with above-ground capacity use near 60.5%, leaving room for further builds.
bullets.vintage: Estimate: early Sep 2026; reported from APPEC; accessed 2026-09-24
bullets.source: MEXC (citing Kayrros chief analyst Antoine Halff at APPEC)

gaps: No single authoritative public series for China's SPR (strategic) inventory changes, estimates rely on satellite/stock-model data.
Current (September 2026) teapot run rates rely on consultancy surveys (Mysteel, JLC, Oilchem) rather than official NBS data, which lags.
Vintage of the exact Russian ESPO/Urals spot premiums could not be fully reconciled across sources; treat as reported.
Whether China's fuel export controls will tighten or loosen further after September is not verifiable.
Whether Beijing issues a third batch of 2026 crude import quotas for independent refiners in Q4, and how much of the 257Mt annual allocation remains unreleased.

No public time series for tank fill levels at new strategic reserve sites; satellite estimates (Kayrros) remain the only near-real-time read, and government vs commercial split is an EIA assumption, not disclosed data.
Aramco's November 2026 official selling prices to Asia (expected around Oct 5) will set the trend for Iranian, Kuwaiti and Iraqi differentials into Q4; direction not verifiable until release.

watches.title: US SPR & Storage Watch
watches.dek: US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) and commercial crude stocks -- SPR inventory, the 2026 exchange/refill mechanics, and Cushing.
watches.how_to_read: Read this page as the US government's sour barrel: the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) is mostly sour crude, and its exchanges put barrels into the market while the returns schedule takes them back out. The reserve's published inventory is the hard data; the 2026 exchange repayment ledger is not published, so outstanding loan balances are estimates. Every bullet carries its vintage.
watches.wcs_stakes: What's drawing lately is leaning sweet: between August 20 and September 11 the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) lost 5.0 million barrels of sweet against 4.2 million of sour, leaving it at roughly 34% sweet and 66% sour against the 40/60 mix the Department of Energy (DOE) says US Gulf Coast refineries were built around, and at 284.9 million barrels the reserve sits only about 32 million above the 252.4-million-barrel minimum Congress mandates. Near term the pressure stays bearish: Energy Secretary Chris Wright calls another exchange round 'a very real possibility' with 38.5 million barrels still unallocated. The trade flips in 2027, when borrowers start returning barrels at about 1.25 per barrel borrowed through 2029, turning the SPR from the market's biggest sour supplier into a standing bid for medium-sour crude.
watches.wcs_closer: For the WCSB book, the SPR is a two-act story with a grade twist: exchanges now, repayments later, and sweet leaving fastest while the reserve drifts further from its 40/60 design mix. Watch the weekly EIA petroleum status report for the draw pace, the DOE grade table for the sweet/sour split, and any disclosed repayments; the 2027-2029 return schedule is a known future bid for sour barrels. Until then, the reserve's releases are the quiet headwind on every sour differential print, and the 252.4-million-barrel congressional floor leaves only about 32 million barrels of drawdown room.

sections.heading: The exchange ledger: two threads, one timeline

bullets.text: Status check on Oct 21: proposals for the 17-million-barrel SPR exchange solicitation issued Oct 16 (FY27 SPR Oil Release No. 1) are due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time today, Oct 21, 2026, and no DOE award announcement for the round had been published on energy.gov as of this check. The DOE newsroom search and the spr.doe.gov exchange pages show no award document for this round and no new SPR exchange or sale authorization since the Oct 10 hurricane emergency exchange; the prior 40-million-barrel round (FY26 SPR Oil Release No. 4, bids closed Oct 6) also still shows no award announcement in the coverage checked. The award announcement for the 17-million-barrel round is the next dated event on the ledger.

Status check on Oct 20: no DOE award announcement for the 17-million-barrel SPR exchange solicitation issued Oct 16 had been published, and no new SPR exchange or sale authorization had followed it. Checked directly on energy.gov: the DOE newsroom's newest press release is dated Oct 19 (a Constitution Pipeline funding item, not SPR), no press release dated Oct 17, 18 or 20 appears in the latest list, and the latest SPR press release remains the Oct 10 hurricane emergency exchange. The spr.doe.gov exchange Active Docs page loaded on this check and shows only the request for proposals and exhibits for FY27 SPR Oil Release No. 1, the up to 17.0-million-barrel round, with no award document listed. Proposals are due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time on Oct 21, 2026. The prior exchanges archive still shows no Award Information link for the earlier 40-million-barrel round, FY26 SPR Oil Release No. 4, whose bids closed Oct 6, unlike the three earlier FY26 rounds. The award announcements are the next dated events on the ledger.

Status check on Oct 19: no DOE award announcement for the 17-million-barrel SPR exchange solicitation issued Oct 16 had been published on energy.gov, and no new SPR exchange or sale authorization had followed it. The DOE newsroom's latest press release is dated Oct 16 and its latest SPR press release remains the Oct 10 hurricane emergency exchange. The 17-million-barrel round, FY27 SPR Oil Release No. 1, is still open, with proposals due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time on Oct 21, 2026. The spr.doe.gov offer system was unreachable during this check, so postings made only on that system could not be verified. The award announcements are the next dated events on the ledger.

The physical shortfall the SPR exchanges are meant to offset deepened last week: intensified attacks on commercial vessels cut Gulf crude flows sharply to about 8.5 million b/d on a seven-day average from more than 20 million b/d the week before, analytics firm Kpler said in a note on Friday cited by Reuters on Oct 19, with at least 10 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels reported last week.

Status check on Oct 18: no DOE award announcement for the 17-million-barrel SPR exchange solicitation issued Oct 16 had been published, and no new SPR exchange or sale authorization had followed it. The round, FY27 SPR Oil Release No. 1, is still open, with proposals due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time on Oct 21, 2026. The earlier 40-million-barrel round, FY26 SPR Oil Release No. 4, whose bids closed Oct 6, also still shows no award information on DOE's exchange archive, unlike the three earlier FY26 rounds. The award announcements are the next dated events on the ledger.

The Department of Energy issued a request for proposals on Oct 16 for an exchange of up to 17 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), Reuters reported. The round is a portion of the pending 40 million barrels that form the last batch of the US 172-million-barrel commitment under the March IEA coordinated release of 400 million barrels. The US has released about 132.5 million barrels from the SPR since the war began. DOE has not published awards from the late September re-offer of the 40 million barrels, but Friday's 17-million-barrel figure implies about 23 million barrels were awarded in that round, Energy Aspects wrote in a note cited by Reuters.

Status check on Oct 16: no DOE award announcement for the sixth and final 40-million-barrel SPR exchange had been published since bids closed Oct 6, and no new SPR exchange or sale authorization had followed the Oct 10 emergency 4-million-barrel Hurricane Isaias exchange. The ledger therefore still stands at up to 44 million barrels committed for November and December delivery, with returns plus premium barrels due from 2027.

Status check on Oct 15: no DOE award announcement for the sixth and final 40-million-barrel SPR exchange had been published since bids closed Oct 6, and no new SPR exchange or sale authorization had followed the Oct 10 emergency 4-million-barrel Hurricane Isaias exchange. The ledger therefore still stands at up to 44 million barrels committed for November and December delivery, with returns plus premium barrels due from 2027.

Two SPR exchange threads are open at once and are tracked here as one ledger. The first is the sixth and final 40-million-barrel exchange under the IEA-coordinated release: bids closed October 6 and the award is still pending. The second is an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels authorized October 10 for Hurricane Isaias disruptions. Combined, up to 44 million barrels of reserve crude is committed to move into the Gulf market in November and December 2026, every barrel a loan due back with premium barrels starting in 2027.

DOE issued the request for proposals for the sixth and final 40-million-barrel exchange, drawn from the Big Hill and Bryan Mound sites, with bids due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time on October 6 and deliveries under awarded exchanges scheduled for November and December 2026. Borrowers return the oil plus premium barrels.
The bid window for the 40-million-barrel exchange closed at 11 a.m. CT. As of October 12, DOE has not announced the award; the award announcement is the next dated event on this ledger.

DOE authorized an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels, 2 million each to ExxonMobil and BP America, to address supply disruptions from Hurricane Isaias. The borrowed crude plus premium barrels is to be returned in 2027; ExxonMobil's share accelerates deliveries of previously awarded SPR crude to keep Gulf Coast refineries running.

Next on the ledger: awarded exchanges under the 40-million-barrel tranche deliver through November and December 2026. Returns begin in 2027, with exchange returns running through 2029; earlier phases returned an average premium of about 25 percent, which DOE says expands long-term reserve inventory at no taxpayer cost.

sections.heading: What's drawing lately: sweet vs sour

bullets.text: DOE's per-site grade table as of August 20, 2026 showed 101.8 million barrels of sweet and 192.3 million of sour (294.1 million total), or roughly 34.6% sweet and 65.4% sour. DOE defines sweet as sulfur content no greater than 0.5% by weight and sour as greater than 0.5% but less than 2.0%; DOE's stated design ratio is about 40% sweet to 60% sour, based on likely US refinery needs, especially on the Gulf Coast.
bullets.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts)

bullets.text: DOE reported the reserve at 284.9 million barrels as of September 11, split 96.8 million sweet and 188.1 million sour (Reuters). Against the August 20 DOE table, sweet drew about 5.0 million barrels and sour about 4.2 million over roughly three weeks, with sweet leaving slightly faster in absolute terms; the sweet share slipped to about 34.0%, drifting further from DOE's 40% design target. Note the September 11 split comes from secondary reporting of a DOE figure, not the published Quick Facts grade table.
bullets.source: Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine)

bullets.text: The September 11 total sat about 32.5 million barrels above the 252.4-million-barrel minimum Congress mandates, so the exchange program has limited drawdown room left before hitting the statutory floor. DOE says it has secured cancellation of 140 million barrels of congressionally mandated sales scheduled for fiscal years 2024 through 2027, so there is no forced-sale overhang on the forward calendar.
bullets.source: Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine); US Department of Energy (energy.gov)

sections.heading: US petroleum stocks: crude, distillate, and gasoline

bullets.text: The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated on Oct 20 that US crude oil inventories fell by 4.93 million barrels in the week ending Oct 16, after an 11.12-million-barrel fall the prior week, OilPrice.com reported. Gasoline inventories fell by 2 million barrels and distillate inventories fell by 2.6 million barrels, on top of a 1.5-million-barrel distillate fall the prior week, while Cushing inventories gained 900,000 barrels after gaining 1.823 million barrels the previous week. Commercial crude inventories excluding the SPR have lost more than 56 million barrels over the last 27 weeks on API data. The official EIA weekly report for the same week is due later on Oct 21.

US crude oil stockpiles were expected to have fallen last week along with product inventories, a preliminary Reuters poll showed on Oct 19, ahead of the next EIA weekly report. The poll follows the Oct 15 EIA report of an 8.6-million-barrel crude draw to 415.6 million barrels in the week ending Oct 9.

EIA reported on Oct 15 that US commercial crude inventories fell 8.6 million barrels to 415.6 million barrels in the week ending Oct 9, against a Reuters poll expectation for a 288,000-barrel draw. Cushing stocks rose 1.9 million barrels, gasoline rose 3.5 million barrels to 208.3 million, distillate fell 2.5 million barrels to 102.6 million, and refinery utilization rose 0.8 points to 93.5 percent. The SPR was unchanged on the week at 283.0 million barrels.

API estimated US crude inventories fell 11.12 million barrels in the week ending Oct 9, after a 2.09-million-barrel fall the prior week, while no barrels left the SPR that week, leaving the reserve at 283 million barrels, still 431 million below maximum capacity. API also put distillate stocks down 1.5 million barrels and gasoline up 1.1 million barrels; official EIA figures were due later on Oct 15.

Gulf of Mexico shut-ins fell sharply by Oct 12 to about 604,503 b/d of oil, 29.63 percent of current daily production, and 531 million cubic feet a day of gas, down from a peak near 1.46 million b/d ahead of Hurricane Isaias landfall, according to the federal offshore regulator's operator reports. Only five production platforms still had personnel evacuated. Shell reported no damage at its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito and Appomattox assets and was redeploying personnel, BP was restarting production at Na Kika and Thunder Horse, and Chevron was restoring full production after curbing five facilities.

Gulf of Mexico oil shut-ins eased to 57.54 percent (about 1.17 million b/d) by Oct 11, down from 62.89 percent on Oct 8, with personnel evacuated from 32 platforms, down sharply from 121 at the storm's peak, as operators began returning crews to undamaged facilities.

Chevron reported it kept production running at four of its nine Gulf platforms through Hurricane Isaias while five were temporarily shut in, and said crew remobilization would continue through Sunday under standard storm recovery procedures at its onshore facilities.

Hurricane Isaias shut in about 1.46 million b/d of Gulf of Mexico oil production with 129 platforms evacuated as the Category 3 storm made landfall late Oct 9 near the Alabama-Florida line; WTI settled at $91.85 and Brent at $104.72 to start the weekend, with the market weighing storm damage against the Hormuz tanker-attack risk.

sections.heading: Distillate: the tightest buffer into winter

bullets.text: Two senior US Energy Department officials said on Oct 20 that Washington is working with refiners in the United States and abroad to increase fuel production as a diesel shortage pushes prices higher, Reuters reported via OilPrice.com. US retail diesel averaged about $6.32 a gallon, with the national average stuck above $6 at record highs. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said earlier this week, as quoted by Reuters: 'We are talking about reopening every refinery we can. There are dialogues there, and that's a tough challenge. I'm not saying all these are going to happen.' The administration has also invoked the Defense Production Act to motivate refiners to restart idle plants, an outcome OilPrice.com noted remains uncertain, and restarting idled refineries takes time and money, so it will not be a quick fix.

The IEA agreed on Oct 15 to accelerate the release of the remaining volumes from its March 2026 collective action, including over 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible, its governing board said after meeting on Thursday. Members had pledged more than 400 million barrels in March. Analysts noted the diesel volume looks like an acceleration of existing commitments rather than new barrels, below the 50 million barrels of diesel discussed earlier in a French proposal.

Details of the Oct 9 Trump-Putin diesel deal now total 4.8 million tons: 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 in November, 1 million after that, and up to 3 million more depending on Russian refinery condition; US diesel futures fell almost 5% to about $4.64 a gallon on the news while AAA's national average sat near a record $6.28.

OFAC General License 135, signed minutes before Trump's Oct 9 announcement, authorizes the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian-origin diesel through 12:01 a.m. EDT on April 7, 2027, while barring debits to US accounts of Russia's central bank, National Wealth Fund and Finance Ministry.

Trump said he would soon issue a directive under the Defense Production Act aimed at expanding US refining capacity; three industry sources told Reuters it could take the form of a presidential memo, as record diesel prices collide with the Iran war's strain on supply.

President Trump announced a deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, plus 500,000 tons in November, 1 million 'immediately thereafter' and 3 million more to follow; Treasury issued a general license sparing Russian diesel loaded as of Oct 9 from sanctions until April 2027, and diesel futures dipped on Friday. The IEA says Russian diesel output has fallen about 30% amid the refinery strikes.

Germany will release up to 15 million barrels of diesel, heating oil and crude from emergency reserves under the G7 plan, Economy Minister Katherina Reiche told Reuters on Friday, the largest European contribution so far; diesel and heating oil go first, with no product breakdown or timeline given.

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said on Oct 8 that member countries still hold about 1.1 billion barrels of public emergency oil stocks, including over 200 million barrels of diesel, and stand ready to release more to the market if and when required.

In a televised national address on Oct 7, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu confirmed France will make 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves available to distributors at cost price over about three months (Nov 2026 to Jan 2027), projected to cut diesel prices at the pump by 12 to 18 euro cents per liter; he will sign a decree authorizing the operation.

Gasoline stocks rose 400,000 barrels (6% below the five-year average) while distillate stocks were essentially unchanged and sit 12% below the five-year average; four-week implied demand averaged 21.1 million b/d, up 0.7% year on year.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 16 that if companies take the full 17 million barrels in the new solicitation before any repayments arrive, SPR inventories would fall from about 283 million barrels to roughly 266 million, inside the 250 to 300 million barrel range generally considered the reserve's operational minimum zone. The June offer of the same final tranche drew agreement to borrow only about 500,000 barrels against premiums of up to 24 percent in extra barrels returned.

The Oct 16 solicitation re-offers the remainder of the final SPR exchange tranche first offered in June, when companies agreed to borrow only about 500,000 barrels against premiums of up to 24 percent in extra barrels returned to the SPR, Reuters reported. Borrowers under an exchange return the crude plus premium barrels at a later date.

The DOE authorized an emergency SPR exchange of up to 4 million barrels (2 million each for ExxonMobil and BP America) to address supply disruptions from Hurricane Isaias, with the borrowed crude plus premium barrels to be returned in 2027. ExxonMobil's share accelerates deliveries of previously awarded SPR crude to keep Gulf Coast refineries running.

The bid window for DOE's sixth and final 40-million-barrel SPR exchange closed on Oct 6 at 11 a.m. CT, with deliveries under awarded exchanges scheduled for November and December 2026; the tranche completes the US portion of the 172-million-barrel pledge under the IEA-coordinated 400-million-barrel release, with borrowers returning the oil plus premium barrels.

The IEA said on Oct 3 that member countries have so far released about 325 million barrels of oil and oil products, more than 80% of the 400 million barrels pledged on March 11, the largest coordinated release in the agency's history. It remains unclear whether the G7's new 100-million-barrel release counts against the roughly 75 million barrels still outstanding under that pledge or comes on top of it.

The Department of Energy issued a request for proposal on Sep 29 for an exchange of up to 40 million barrels of SPR crude from the Big Hill and Bryan Mound sites, with deliveries under awarded exchanges scheduled for November and December 2026 and bids due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time on Oct 6; DOE says five prior solicitations awarded more than 133 million barrels and earlier exchanges returned an average 25 percent premium.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright clarified in a CNBC interview that Venezuela's heavy crude would not be placed directly into reserve salt caverns but could be swapped for light or medium US barrels, because much of Venezuela's oil is heavier and higher in sulfur than the crude traditionally held in the reserve. Analysts quoted in the piece cautioned that many of the Venezuelan fields would need years of development and reinvestment before producing meaningful volumes.

In June 2026 the Department of Energy (DOE) awarded contracts for a further approximately 53.3 million barrels of Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) exchange crude across all four sites (Bayou Choctaw, Bryan Mound, Big Hill, West Hackberry) under its late-April request for proposal, carrying an approximately 28 percent return premium (15.1 million barrels). DOE said about 35 million barrels had been delivered to market to that point and that earlier phases had awarded roughly 80 million barrels (45.2 plus 8.5 plus 26 million).

Other International Energy Agency (IEA) members' announced contributions to the 400-million-barrel coordinated release included 22.46 million barrels from South Korea and 13.5 million barrels from the United Kingdom, with Germany, Austria, and Japan also releasing stock (Japan's releases began in mid-March), per reporting in late July 2026. Aggregate member delivery progress beyond these pledges has not been published in a single authoritative ledger.

Federal law restricts non-emergency drawdowns once SPR inventories fall below 252.4 million barrels, and a 1981 GAO report advised against releases below 250 million except in a very severe emergency. With the reserve near 284 million barrels and another tranche now in motion, the legal floor is roughly 30 million barrels away.

In the same API report on Oct 20, 300,000 barrels of crude oil left the SPR in the week ending Oct 16, taking the SPR total down to 282.7 million barrels, OilPrice.com reported, still 431 million barrels below maximum capacity and inside the 250 to 300 million barrel range generally considered the reserve's operational minimum zone. That follows the DOE data that put the SPR at 283 million barrels as of Oct 9, the lowest since October 1982.

DOE data released on Oct 13 put the SPR at 283 million barrels as of Oct 9, unchanged from the prior week and still the lowest since October 1982, about 13 million barrels above the first reading in August 1982. Senator Martin Heinrich raised concerns about salt cavern integrity at current low levels, while the administration said the caverns can be managed safely.

The SPR fell another 784,000 barrels to 283.0 million barrels, taking cumulative withdrawals since late March to 132.5 million barrels; combined commercial and SPR crude stocks drew 3.97 million barrels in the week.

Stocks of crude oil in the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to 283 million barrels in the week ending Oct 2, the lowest level since October 1982, according to Department of Energy data reported by Reuters. The drawdowns are part of the U.S. agreement to release 172 million barrels under the IEA coordinated action, and the administration last week offered to loan energy companies a further 40 million barrels from the reserve.
